intro: The basement holds the foundations the rest of the course stands on. Every exam starts here: probability current and continuity (FS22 Q1), Ehrenfest (HS21 Q1, FS19 Q2), the box with a symmetry operator or an expansion (FS26 Q2, FS19 Q1). The pattern is always the same: write down eigenstates, expand, square the coefficients, check that the probabilities add up to one.

tutorial.title: The well and the packet
tutorial.html: On the back wall the infinite well of width $a$ with the two lowest levels. The glowing curve is $|\Psi|^2$ for $\frac1{\sqrt2}(\psi_1+\psi_2)$: the density sloshes back and forth with the angular frequency $(E_2-E_1)/\hbar$, while the density of a single eigenstate would stand still.

tutorial.title: The spreading packet
tutorial.html: In front of the well a free Gaussian packet widens as $\Delta x(t)=\Delta x_0\sqrt{1+(\hbar\lambda t/m)^2}$ while the area under $|\Psi|^2$ stays one. The narrower it starts, the faster it spreads: this is $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$ in motion.

tutorial.title: Consoles
tutorial.html: Library: Compton to Ehrenfest and the box. Quiz: eight multiple-choice questions. Derivation desk: Compton, continuity, Ehrenfest, Gaussian spreading, the sudden wall. Fights: Compton, spreading, sudden wall. Boss gate: FS26 Q2, FS19 Q1, FS22 Q1.

encounters.title: From photons to matter waves: Compton, de Broglie, the Bohr orbit

source.where: Q1 Compton, Q2 Bohr atom and de Broglie

blocks.html: Photon as particle. A photon of wavelength $\lambda$ carries the four-momentum $p^\mu=(\hbar k,\hbar\vec k)$, $k=\omega/c=2\pi/\lambda$ (script 1.23). In Compton scattering off an electron at rest, energy and momentum conservation (square the electron momentum to eliminate its angle) give a wavelength shift that depends only on the scattering angle:

Classical (Thomson) scattering predicts no shift: the driven electron radiates at the driving frequency. The shift is visible only if $\lambda_C$ is a noticeable fraction of $\lambda$: hard X-rays ($\lambda\sim10^{-11}$ m) yes, visible light ($10^{-7}$ m, relative shift $\lesssim10^{-4}$) no.
Matter as wave. De Broglie postulates the same relation for particles (script 1.24, 2.1):

blocks.label: Davisson-Germer confirmed it with electron diffraction on a crystal

blocks.html: Bohr orbits as standing waves (sheet I Q2). Bohr's quantisation $mv_nr_n=n\hbar$ is the same as $2\pi r_n=n\lambda$: the de Broglie wave closes on itself, $\lambda/r_n=2\pi\hbar/(mv_nr_n)=2\pi/n$. With $r_n=n^2a_0$ and $v_n=\alpha c/n$ the electron is non-relativistic ($v_1=2.19\times10^6$ m/s, $v_1/c=1/137$), so $p=mv$ is justified.
Quantisation is a resonance condition: only waves that fit survive. This is the seed of the box spectrum (lesson 4): $n\lambda/2=a$.

(1) Compton shifts the wavelength, not the frequency of the scattered light by a classical factor; the shift is independent of $\lambda_1$. (2) $\lambda_C=h/mc$ uses the electron mass; the photon has no rest mass. (3) $hc=1239.84$ eV nm is the quickest route from photon energy to wavelength.

Sheet I (Gaberdiel HS25), Q1-Q2: derive the Compton formula from four-momentum conservation, explain why Thomson scattering is the limit $\lambda\gg h/mc$, and check $2\pi r_n=n\lambda$ for the Bohr orbits.

Why is the Compton effect not seen with visible light?
options: $\lambda_C/\lambda\sim10^{-5}$: the relative shift is far below what a spectrometer resolves
energy conservation fails for visible light

check.q: In the Bohr model, de Broglie's relation turns $mv_nr_n=n\hbar$ into
options: $2\pi r_n=n\lambda$: $n$ wavelengths fit around the orbit

encounters.title: Schroedinger equation, probability current, Galilean invariance, Ehrenfest

blocks.html: From $\lambda=2\pi\hbar/p$ and $\omega=E/\hbar$ one gets $\partial_x\Psi=\frac{ip}\hbar\Psi$ and $\partial_t\Psi=-\frac{iE}\hbar\Psi$; with $E=p^2/2m+V$ the postulate (script 2.7) is $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=\big(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2+V\big)\Psi$, $p=-i\hbar\partial_x$. Born: $\rho=|\Psi|^2$ with $\int\rho\,dx=1$ at all times.

Continuity equation (FS22 Q1(i), 4 pt). Use the equation and its complex conjugate in $\partial_t\rho=\Psi^*\dot\Psi+\Psi\dot\Psi^*$; the $V$ terms cancel because $V$ is real, the rest is a total derivative:

Examples. $\Psi=Ae^{ikx/\hbar}e^{-iEt/\hbar}$ gives $j=|A|^2k/m$ (density times velocity). The superposition $Ae^{ikx/\hbar}+Be^{-ikx/\hbar}$ gives $j=(|A|^2-|B|^2)k/m$: the interference term drops out of $j$ (sheet II Q3). A real stationary wavefunction has $j=0$. For $E
Galilean invariance (sheet I Q3). If $\Psi(x,t)$ solves the free equation then so does the boosted wave. The phase factor is needed because $p\to p+mu$:

blocks.label: check: the cross term -i hbar u dPsi/dx cancels the time derivative of the shifted argument

blocks.html: Ehrenfest theorem. $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac1m\langle p\rangle$ and $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle\partial_xV\rangle$ (script 2.25-2.26). In Dirac notation (HS21 Q1) it is a commutator statement: $\frac d{dt}\langle A\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[H,A]\rangle$ with $[H,x]=-\frac{i\hbar}mp$ and $[H,p]=i\hbar V'(x)$.

The centre of the packet obeys Newton's law only with the average force $\langle V'(x)\rangle$, not the force at the average position $V'(\langle x\rangle)$. They agree exactly for $V$ at most quadratic (harmonic oscillator: $\langle x\rangle$ follows the classical orbit for any state).

(1) $j$ has the sign convention $\Psi\partial\Psi^*-\Psi^*\partial\Psi$ with prefactor $+\frac{i\hbar}{2m}$ in the script; swapping the order flips the sign. (2) The boost phase carries $-\frac12u^2t$: forgetting it breaks the time derivative. (3) Ehrenfest does not say $\langle x\rangle$ obeys the classical equation for anharmonic $V$.
FS22 Q1 (17 pt): continuity equation, current of a plane wave, current for a step with $E>V_0$ and the check $\partial_xj=0$, and $j=0$ for $E<V_0$. HS21 Q1 (10 pt) and FS19 Q2(i) (5 pt): Ehrenfest.

check.explain: Each plane wave gives $\pm|\cdot|^2k/m$ and the cross terms cancel.

check.q: The boosted free solution $\Psi_u$ needs the phase $\exp[\frac{im}\hbar(ux-\frac12u^2t)]$ because
options: momentum and energy shift as $p\to p+mu$, $E\to E+up+\frac12mu^2$
the potential changes under the boost
check.explain: Check: $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi_u$ and $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2\Psi_u$ differ by $-i\hbar u\Psi'$ and $\frac m2u^2\Psi$ terms which the phase supplies.

check.q: Ehrenfest: $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle V'(x)\rangle$. For $V=\frac12m\omega^2x^2$ this equals $-m\omega^2\langle x\rangle$, because
options: $V'$ is linear in $x$, so $\langle V'(x)\rangle=V'(\langle x\rangle)$
check.explain: Average of a linear function = function of the average.

encounters.title: The Gaussian packet: uncertainty and free spreading

blocks.html: Sheet III Q1: $\Psi=Ae^{-\lambda x^2/2}$. Normalisation $\int|\Psi|^2dx=|A|^2\sqrt{\pi/\lambda}=1$ gives $A=(\lambda/\pi)^{1/4}$. Gaussian integrals give $\langle x\rangle=0$, $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac1{2\lambda}$ and, with $p=-i\hbar\partial_x$, $\langle p\rangle=0$, $\langle p^2\rangle=\hbar^2\!\int|\Psi'|^2=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda}2$.

The same $\Psi$ solves the stationary equation for $V=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda^2}{2m}x^2$ with $E=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda}{2m}$: it is the oscillator ground state with $\lambda=m\omega/\hbar$, $E=\hbar\omega/2$. A tighter trap (large $\lambda$) means small $\Delta x$, large $\Delta p$ and large kinetic energy $\langle p^2\rangle/2m=\hbar^2\lambda/4m$.

Free spreading. Expand in plane waves, $\Psi(x,t)=\int dp\,\phi(p)e^{ipx/\hbar-ip^2t/2m\hbar}$. Each component has phase velocity $p/2m$ but the packet moves with the group velocity $d\omega/dk=p/m$. For the Gaussian the Fresnel-type integral can be done in closed form with $\tau=\hbar\lambda t/m$:

Reading it: $|\Psi|^2\propto\exp[-\lambda x^2/(1+\tau^2)]$ stays Gaussian and its width grows like $\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$, while $\Delta p$ is constant (free evolution does not change $|\phi(p)|^2$). Equivalent kinematic form: $\Delta x(t)^2=\Delta x_0^2+(\Delta p\,t/m)^2$, the spread of velocities $\Delta p/m$ times time. The spreading time is $t_*=m/(\hbar\lambda)=2m\Delta x_0^2/\hbar$.

An electron localised to $\Delta x_0=1$ Å has $\Delta v=\hbar/(2m\Delta x_0)\approx5.8\times10^5$ m/s and doubles its width in $t=\sqrt3\,t_*\approx3\times10^{-16}$ s. A 1 g marble localised to 1 $\mu$m has $t_*\sim10^{19}$ s, about $10^{12}$ years. Spreading is real for microscopic particles only.

(1) The minimum-uncertainty product holds at $t=0$ only; for $t>0$ it grows, $\Delta x\Delta p=\frac\hbar2\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$. (2) The phase velocity of a plane wave is half the particle velocity; the particle moves with the group velocity. (3) $\langle p^2\rangle$ needs $\int|\Psi'|^2$, not $|\Psi|^2p^2$; do not insert $p=\hbar k$ blindly for a packet.
Sheet III Q1 and HS18 Q2: compute $\Delta x,\Delta p$ of a Gaussian and interpret the energy cost of localisation; spreading is the free-particle analogue.

check.q: A free Gaussian packet has $\Delta x(0)=\Delta x_0$. At large times $\Delta x(t)$ grows as
During free spreading of the Gaussian packet $\Delta p$ is
options: decreasing, since the packet gets broader in $x$
check.explain: Free $H=p^2/2m$ commutes with $p$, so the distribution of $p$ is conserved.

check.q: Sheet III Q1(iv): making $\Delta x\to0$ with a Gaussian costs
options: a finite energy $\hbar\omega/2$ for any width
check.explain: Localisation and kinetic energy are tied by $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$.

encounters.title: The box: eigenstates, expansion, 2D box and the suddenly moved wall

blocks.html: $V=0$ on $[0,a]$, $\infty$ outside forces $\psi(0)=\psi(a)=0$ (only $\psi$ is continuous). Solutions with $E\le0$ cannot satisfy both conditions; $E>0$ gives $\sin kx$ with $ka=n\pi$:

blocks.label: script Ch. 3.1; ground state energy > 0 is the uncertainty principle

blocks.html: Expansion and measurement. $\Psi(x,t)=\sum_nc_n\psi_ne^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$, $c_n=\int\psi_n^*\Psi(x,0)\,dx$, and a measurement of $H$ gives $E_n$ with $P_n=|c_n|^2$, leaving the state $\psi_n$ (script 2.7 postulate). Sheet III Q2: $\Psi(x,0)=1/\sqrt a$ gives $P_n=\frac8{n^2\pi^2}$ for odd $n$, $0$ for even $n$ (the state is symmetric about $a/2$, $\psi_n$ has parity $(-1)^{n+1}$). The same idea gives $\sum_{n\ \text{odd}}n^{-2}=\pi^2/8$ and $\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$. Moments: $(\Delta x)^2=\frac{a^2}{12}\big(1-\frac6{n^2\pi^2}\big)$, which tends to the classical uniform value $a^2/12$.

2D box (FS19 Q1). The Hamiltonian separates: $\psi_{n_xn_y}=\frac2a\sin\frac{n_x\pi x}a\sin\frac{n_y\pi y}a$, $E=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2ma^2}(n_x^2+n_y^2)$. The exchange $R\Psi(x,y)=\Psi(y,x)$ commutes with $H$ ($R^2=1$, eigenvalues $\pm1$); degenerate pairs $(n_x,n_y)\ne(n_y,n_x)$ are split into the combinations $\frac1{\sqrt2}(\psi_{n_xn_y}\pm\psi_{n_yn_x})$ with $R=\pm1$, while $(n,n)$ has $R=+1$.

Sudden wall change (sheet III Q4). The wall moves instantly from $a$ to $2a$: the wavefunction cannot change in zero time, so $\Psi(x,0^+)=\psi_1^{(a)}(x)$ (zero on $[a,2a]$), but the eigenstates are now $\phi_n=\frac1{\sqrt a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{2a}$, $E_n'=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{8ma^2}$. Overlap with $c_n=\int_0^a\phi_n\psi_1^{(a)}dx$:

$E_2'=\pi^2\hbar^2/(2ma^2)$ is exactly the old energy $E_1$: with probability $\tfrac12$ the sudden expansion changes nothing; the remaining $\tfrac12$ is spread over odd $n$ (the energy expectation $\langle H\rangle$ is unchanged, as no work is done by a sudden change).

(1) Use the new eigenfunctions $\phi_n$ and the old state; mixing $a$ and $2a$ in the normalisation is the typical slip. (2) Parity is about the box centre $a/2$, not $x=0$. (3) After an energy measurement the state is $\psi_n$ (not a superposition), and then only $e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$ is left.

FS26 Q2 (20 pt): box eigenfunctions, parity operator $(P\psi)(x)=\psi(a-x)$, $P_n$ for $\psi=\sqrt{30/a^5}\,x(a-x)$ and $\sum_l(2l+1)^{-6}=\pi^6/960$. FS19 Q1 (21 pt): 2D box with exchange operator $R$.

encounters.title: Compton scattering: the wavelength shift (sheet I Q1)
encounters.goal: Derive $\lambda_2-\lambda_1=\frac h{mc}(1-\cos\theta)$ for a photon scattered by an electron at rest.
given: photon $p^\mu=(\hbar k,\hbar\vec k)$ with $k=2\pi/\lambda$ (energy $\hbar kc$), electron initially at rest, relativistic $E_e^2=p_e^2c^2+m^2c^4$
energy and momentum conservation, scattering angle $\theta$ between $\vec k_1$ and $\vec k_2$

steps.reveal: Energy: $\hbar k_1c+mc^2=\hbar k_2c+E_e$. Momentum: $\hbar\vec k_1=\hbar\vec k_2+\vec p_e$.

steps.prompt: (b) Eliminate the unknown electron angle: square the momentum law.
steps.reveal: $p_e^2=\hbar^2(\vec k_1-\vec k_2)^2=\hbar^2(k_1^2+k_2^2-2k_1k_2\cos\theta)$.

steps.prompt: (c) Square the energy law solved for $E_e$ and use $E_e^2=p_e^2c^2+m^2c^4$.
steps.reveal: $E_e=\hbar c(k_1-k_2)+mc^2$, so $E_e^2=\hbar^2c^2(k_1-k_2)^2+2mc^2\hbar c(k_1-k_2)+m^2c^4$. Equate with $\hbar^2c^2(k_1^2+k_2^2-2k_1k_2\cos\theta)+m^2c^4$.

The $E_e^2$ and $m^2c^4$ terms: the squares $k_1^2,k_2^2$ cancel, leaving $-2k_1k_2\hbar^2c^2+2mc^3\hbar(k_1-k_2)=-2k_1k_2\hbar^2c^2\cos\theta$, i.e. $mc\,(k_1-k_2)=\hbar k_1k_2(1-\cos\theta)$. Divide by $k_1k_2$: $\frac1{k_2}-\frac1{k_1}=\frac\hbar{mc}(1-\cos\theta)$. With $k=2\pi/\lambda$: $\lambda_2-\lambda_1=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{mc}(1-\cos\theta)=\frac h{mc}(1-\cos\theta)$.

keyPoints: two conservation laws, three unknowns reduce to one by squaring
no electron angle appears in the result

encounters.title: Continuity equation and probability current (FS22 Q1 (i))

steps.reveal: $\partial_t\rho=\Psi^*\partial_t\Psi+\Psi\,\partial_t\Psi^*$.

$\partial_t\Psi=\frac1{i\hbar}\big(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Psi''+V\Psi\big)$, $\partial_t\Psi^*=-\frac1{i\hbar}\big(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Psi^{*\prime\prime}+V\Psi^*\big)$. The $V$ terms cancel because $V$ is real.

steps.prompt: (c) Collect the second-derivative terms as a total derivative.
steps.reveal: $\partial_t\rho=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\big(\Psi^*\Psi''-\Psi\Psi^{*\prime\prime}\big)=\partial_x\Big[\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\big(\Psi^*\Psi'-\Psi\Psi^{*\prime}\big)\Big]$, since the cross terms $\Psi^{*\prime}\Psi'$ cancel.

steps.prompt: (d) Define $j$ and check a plane wave.
steps.reveal: $j=\frac{i\hbar}{2m}\big(\Psi\,\partial_x\Psi^*-\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi\big)=\frac\hbar m\,\mathrm{Im}(\Psi^*\partial_x\Psi)$ (script 2.16), so $\partial_t\rho+\partial_xj=0$. For $\Psi=Ae^{ikx/\hbar}$: $j=|A|^2k/m$ ($k$ is a momentum).

keyPoints: real potential makes the $V$ terms cancel
second-derivative terms form a total derivative

encounters.title: Ehrenfest's theorem (HS21 Q1, FS19 Q2 (i))

source.where: Question 1 (ii)-(iv), 5 pt; also FS 19 Aufgabe 2 (i), 5 pt

encounters.goal: Show $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac1m\langle p\rangle$ and $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle V'(x)\rangle$.

steps.prompt: (a) Differentiate $\langle x\rangle=\langle\psi|x|\psi\rangle$ and insert the Schroedinger equation and its adjoint.
steps.reveal: $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle\psi|Hx|\psi\rangle-\frac i\hbar\langle\psi|xH|\psi\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[H,x]\rangle$.
$V$ commutes with $x$; $[p^2,x]=p[p,x]+[p,x]p=-2i\hbar p$. Hence $[H,x]=\frac{1}{2m}(-2i\hbar p)=-\frac{i\hbar}mp$.
$\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac i\hbar\cdot\big(-\frac{i\hbar}m\big)\langle p\rangle=\frac1m\langle p\rangle$.

steps.prompt: (d) Repeat for $p$ and state the classical limit.
steps.reveal: $\frac d{dt}\langle p\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[H,p]\rangle$ with $[V(x),p]=i\hbar V'(x)$, so $\frac d{dt}\langle p\rangle=-\langle V'(x)\rangle$ and $m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\langle x\rangle=-\langle V'(x)\rangle$. This equals Newton's law for $\langle x\rangle$ only if $\langle V'(x)\rangle=V'(\langle x\rangle)$, exactly true for $V$ at most quadratic (harmonic oscillator).

keyPoints: mean values obey Newton only if $\langle V'(x)\rangle=V'(\langle x\rangle)$

encounters.title: Free spreading of a Gaussian packet (sheet III Q1)

source.where: Question 1 (Gaussian wave function); free spreading extends it, script Ch. 2

given: $\Delta x_0^2=\frac1{2\lambda}$, momentum space $\tilde\Psi(p)\propto e^{-p^2/2\hbar^2\lambda}$, so $\Delta p^2=\frac{\hbar^2\lambda}2$
free evolution: each momentum component gets the phase $e^{-ip^2t/2m\hbar}$

steps.prompt: (a) Why is $\Delta p$ constant in time?
steps.reveal: $H=p^2/2m$ commutes with $p$, so $|\tilde\Psi(p,t)|^2=|\tilde\Psi(p,0)|^2$ and $\Delta p^2=\hbar^2\lambda/2$ forever.
$\Psi(x,t)\propto\int dp\,e^{-p^2(1/2\hbar^2\lambda+it/2m\hbar)+ipx/\hbar}$: a Gaussian with complex width $\frac1{\lambda}\to\frac1\lambda+\frac{i\hbar t}m$.

steps.prompt: (c) Evaluate and read off the width.
steps.reveal: $|\Psi(x,t)|^2\propto\exp\!\big[-\frac{\lambda x^2}{1+(\hbar\lambda t/m)^2}\big]$, a Gaussian with $\Delta x^2=\frac{1+(\hbar\lambda t/m)^2}{2\lambda}$.

$\Delta x(t)^2=\Delta x_0^2+(\Delta p\,t/m)^2$: initial width plus the ballistic spread of the momentum distribution. $\Delta x\,\Delta p=\frac\hbar2\sqrt{1+(\hbar\lambda t/m)^2}\ge\hbar/2$, the packet is minimal only at $t=0$.

keyPoints: $\Delta p$ is conserved for a free particle

encounters.title: Sudden wall: box $[0,a]\to[0,2a]$ (sheet III Q4)

source.where: Question 4, box whose wall is suddenly moved

encounters.goal: A particle in the ground state of a box of width $a$ finds its wall moved suddenly to $2a$. Find the probabilities $P_n$ of energies of the new box.
given: old: $\psi_1=\sqrt{2/a}\sin(\pi x/a)$ on $[0,a]$; new: $\phi_n=\sqrt{1/a}\sin(n\pi x/2a)$ on $[0,2a]$
sudden change: the wave function does not change, $P_n=|\langle\phi_n|\psi_1\rangle|^2$

steps.reveal: $c_n=\int_0^a\phi_n\psi_1\,dx=\frac{\sqrt2}a\int_0^a\sin\frac{\pi x}a\sin\frac{n\pi x}{2a}dx$ (the old state vanishes for $x>a$).
$\sin\frac{2\pi x}{2a}=\sin\frac{\pi x}a$, so $c_2=\frac{\sqrt2}a\int_0^a\sin^2\frac{\pi x}a=\frac{\sqrt2}a\cdot\frac a2=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $P_2=\frac12$.

$\sin A\sin B=\frac12[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)]$ gives $\int_0^a=\frac a{\pi}\Big[\frac{\sin((n-2)\pi/2)}{n-2}-\frac{\sin((n+2)\pi/2)}{n+2}\Big]$. Even $n\neq2$: both sines vanish. Odd $n$: the sines are equal, so $\int_0^a=\frac{4a}\pi\frac{\sin((n-2)\pi/2)}{n^2-4}$.
$P_n=\frac{32}{\pi^2(n^2-4)^2}$ for odd $n$, $P_2=\frac12$, $P_{\text{even}\ne2}=0$. E.g. $P_1=\frac{32}{9\pi^2}=0.360$. Normalisation: $\frac12+\sum_{n\text{ odd}}P_n=1$.

keyPoints: sudden change: project the old state on the new eigenstates

encounters.title: Compton shift of an X-ray photon (sheet I Q1)
encounters.problem: An X-ray photon scatters off a free electron at rest and emerges at angle $\theta$ to its original direction. Find the wavelength shift and evaluate it at $\theta=90^\circ$. Source: sheet I Q1; numbers are an adaptation chosen for the game.

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: Energy and momentum conservation with relativistic electron energy; square the electron momentum to remove the electron angle.

steps.prompt: Why can the shift not be explained by classical (Thomson) scattering?
options: because the electron is too heavy
the classical electron radiates at the driving frequency, so $\lambda_2=\lambda_1$; the shift needs photon momentum $\hbar k$
because the shift depends on the intensity

why.0: The shift is $\propto1/m$, but the classical wave picture gives exactly zero for any $m$.
why.2: Wave properties are used in diffraction; the failing piece is the energy-momentum transfer to a single electron.
why.3: The shift depends only on the angle, not on intensity.

items.why: Starting point, nothing to eliminate yet.

items.text: Square the momentum law to get $p_e^2$ without the electron angle
items.why: Only the photon angle $\theta$ should survive.

steps.hint: conservation, eliminate the electron angle, equate energies, convert to wavelengths.
$\lambda_C=h/mc$ is a length; the angular factor $1-\cos\theta$ runs from $0$ (forward) to $2$ (backward).

steps.prompt: Bonus: the shift at $\theta=90^\circ$ in pm (use h, m, c in SI and multiply by $10^{12}$).
steps.hint: $h/mc=2.426\times10^{-12}$ m, and $1-\cos90^\circ=1$, so the shift is $2.43$ pm.

encounters.title: How fast does a localised electron spread? (sheet III Q1, free evolution)
encounters.problem: An electron is prepared in the Gaussian $\Psi(x,0)=(\lambda/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-\lambda x^2/2}$ with initial width $\Delta x_0=1$ Angstrom and then moves freely. Find $\Delta x(t)$ and the time after which the width has grown by the factor $\sqrt2$. Source: sheet III Q1 extended by free evolution (adaptation).

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: $\Delta p$ is constant, the position width grows ballistically: $\Delta x^2=\Delta x_0^2+(\Delta p\,t/m)^2$ with $\Delta p=\hbar/(2\Delta x_0)$.

steps.prompt: Which statement about $\Delta p$ is true during free evolution?
options: $\Delta p$ shrinks, since the packet becomes more classical

why.1: $|\tilde\Psi(p,t)|^2$ is time independent; only the phases of momentum components change.
why.2: The uncertainty product grows, but $\Delta p$ itself is conserved.
why.3: A localised packet needs a spread of momenta.

items.why: Free evolution is diagonal in momentum space.

items.text: Do the Gaussian integral back to position space

items.why: Last: the width follows from the modulus squared.

steps.prompt: Bonus: the time (in attoseconds) when $\Delta x=\sqrt2\,\Delta x_0$ for $\Delta x_0=10^{-10}$ m (dx).
steps.hint: $\hbar\lambda t/m=1$ with $\lambda=1/2\Delta x_0^2$ gives $t=2m\Delta x_0^2/\hbar=1.73\times10^{-16}$ s $=173$ as.

encounters.title: The suddenly moved wall (sheet III Q4)
encounters.problem: A particle is in the ground state of a box $[0,a]$. The right wall is suddenly moved to $2a$. Find the probability $P_n$ to measure the new energy $E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{8ma^2}$ and evaluate $P_1$. Source: sheet III Q4.
symbols: quantum number in the new box (odd)

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: Sudden approximation: the wave function stays $\psi_1$ (zero for $x>a$). Expand it in $\phi_n=\frac1{\sqrt a}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{2a}$.

steps.prompt: Which wave function is expanded right after the move?
options: the old $\psi_1$, extended by zero on $[a,2a]$

why.0: The new ground state is the result of a slow (adiabatic) expansion, not of a sudden one.
why.1: Stretching would be adiabatic; suddenly the function has no time to change.
why.2: The wave function is continuous in time; the energy is not a property of it before the measurement.

items.why: The two sines coincide, the general formula has a $0/0$.

items.text: For $n\ne2$ use product-to-sum; even $n$ gives $0$, odd $n$ gives $\frac{4\sqrt2\sin(n\pi/2)}{\pi(4-n^2)}$

steps.hint: $c_n=\frac{4\sqrt2\sin(n\pi/2)}{\pi(4-n^2)}$ for odd $n$; the sign drops out when squaring.
$P_1=\frac{32}{9\pi^2}=0.360$; with $P_2=\frac12$ and $P_3=0.130$ the first three terms give $0.99$.

encounters.title: Particle in the box with the reflection P (FS26 Q2)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer. Enter the probabilities and the sum. The statement below is the exam text (formulas shortened where marked).
statement: Consider a particle in 1d, confined to a box of length $a$. The Hamiltonian is $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2+V(x)$ with $V=0$ for $x\in[0,a]$ and $V=\infty$ else.

(i) Find the (normalised) eigenfunctions $\psi_n$ and the associated eigenvalues $E_n$ of the Hamiltonian for the particle in the box. What boundary conditions does the wave function have to satisfy? [5 points]
(ii) Consider the operator $P$ which acts as $(P\psi)(x)=\psi(a-x)$. Show that $P$ is a symmetry of the Hamiltonian, and that the eigenfunctions of $H$ are eigenfunctions of $P$. [4 points]
Let the wave function of the particle be $\psi(x)=\sqrt{30/a^5}\,x(a-x)$. (iii) We can write it as $\psi(x)=\sum_nc_n\psi_n(x)$. Which $c_n$ are allowed to be non-zero by the symmetry $P$? [3 points]

(iv) The energy of the particle in this state is measured. Calculate the probability that one measures the energy $E_n$. Hint: you may use $\int_0^1dy\,y\sin(\pi ny)=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\pi n}$ and $\int_0^1dy\,y^2\sin(\pi ny)=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\pi n}-2\frac{1-(-1)^n}{\pi^3n^3}$. [5 points]
(v) Use the previous result to show that $\sum_{l=0}^\infty\frac1{(2l+1)^6}=\frac{\pi^6}{960}$. [3 points]

finalAnswers.prompt: (iv) $P_1$, the probability of the ground-state energy $E_1$.
(iii)/(v) Sum of $P_n$ over all odd $n$ (what must the symmetry argument give?).
(v) The value of $\sum_{l\ge0}(2l+1)^{-6}$ to four digits.

keyPoints: (ii) $V$ is symmetric under $x\to a-x$ and $\partial_x^2$ is invariant, so $[P,H]=0$; $\psi_n(a-x)=(-1)^{n+1}\psi_n(x)$
(iii) $\psi$ is symmetric ($P=+1$), so only odd $n$ contribute

encounters.title: Particle in a 2d box (FS19 Q1)

source.where: Question 1 [Particle in a 2d box, 21 pt] (English version of Aufgabe 1)

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer. In (ii)-(v) the game fixes $A=\frac12$, $B=\frac i2$, $C=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ (adaptation: the exam keeps $A,B,C$ general with $|A|^2+|B|^2+|C|^2=1$). Energies are in units of $\pi^2\hbar^2/2ma^2$.
statement: We consider a particle of mass $m$ moving in a 2-dimensional box of size $a$ with coordinates $0\le x\le a$ and $0\le y\le a$. The potential vanishes inside the box, and the wave function vanishes at the edges.
(i) Find the normalised eigenfunctions of the Hamilton operator and the associated energies. [6 pt]

(ii) At $t=0$ the system is described by $\Psi(x,y)=\frac{2A}a\sin\frac{2\pi x}a\sin\frac{\pi y}a+\frac{2B}a\sin\frac{\pi x}a\sin\frac{2\pi y}a+\frac{2C}a\sin\frac{\pi x}a\sin\frac{\pi y}a$ with complex $A,B,C$, $|A|^2+|B|^2+|C|^2=1$. Give the wave function for $t>0$. [2 pt]
(iii) At $t_1>0$ the energy is measured. What are the possible outcomes and probabilities? In each case describe the wave function immediately after the measurement. [4 pt]

(iv) The Hamiltonian commutes with the operator $R$ that exchanges $x$ and $y$, $R\Psi(x,y)=\Psi(y,x)$. Show that $R$ is hermitian and determine its eigenvalues. Find a basis of simultaneous normalised eigenfunctions of $H$ and $R$. [4 pt]

(v) At $t_1>0$, $R$ is measured for the state of (ii) (system undisturbed for $0\le t\le t_1$). What values of $R$ can be found, with which probabilities? Describe the wave function directly after the measurement. [5 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: (iii) Probability to measure $E=5$ (units above) for the given $A,B,C$.

keyPoints: (ii) multiply each term by $e^{-iEt/\hbar}$: $E_{21}=E_{12}=5\epsilon$ share the phase, $E_{11}=2\epsilon$
(iii) $P(5\epsilon)=|A|^2+|B|^2$ with the projected state $(A\psi_{21}+B\psi_{12})/\sqrt{|A|^2+|B|^2}$; $P(2\epsilon)=|C|^2$ with state $\psi_{11}$
(iv) $\langle\Phi|R\Psi\rangle=\langle R\Phi|\Psi\rangle$ by relabelling $x\leftrightarrow y$, $R^2=1$ so $R=\pm1$; basis $\psi_{nn}$, $(\psi_{nm}\pm\psi_{mn})/\sqrt2$

encounters.title: Wave mechanics: current and the potential step (FS22 Q1)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer. For (iii) the game uses $E=2V_0$ and unit incoming amplitude (adaptation: the exam asks for the general solution). Currents are in units of $k/m$ with $k=\sqrt{2mE}$.
statement: Let $\Psi(x,t)$ be a solution of the time-dependent Schroedinger equation (one dimension). The probability density is $\rho(x,t)=|\Psi(x,t)|^2$.
(i) Show the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\partial_xj=0$, where $j$ is the probability current that you should define. [4 pt]

(ii) For a free particle of mass $m$ ($V=0$) state the most general (non-normalised) solution of the time-dependent Schroedinger equation with energy $E=\frac{k^2}{2m}$. Determine the probability current of this solution. [4 pt]

(iii) Consider $V(x)=0$ for $x<0$ and $V(x)=V_0>0$ for $x>0$. Derive the most general (non-normalised) solution of the time-independent Schroedinger equation with energy $E>V_0$, describing an incoming particle from the left. Determine the probability current of this solution and confirm that the continuity equation holds. [7 pt]
(iv) For $E<V_0$, briefly argue that the probability current vanishes. [2 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: (iii) $j_{\text{trans}}$ in units of $k/m$ (equal to $1-|r|^2$ by the continuity equation).
(iii) Total current for $x<0$ in units of $k/m$ (must equal the transmitted one).

keyPoints: (iv) for $E<V_0$ the solution for $x>0$ is real up to a constant phase ($e^{-\kappa x}$), so $\mathrm{Im}(\psi^*\psi')=0$; on the left $|r|=1$
